flows.title: gdgraph provenance never advances after a metaproject-only commit, so the wiki baseline can never be recorded
criteria: AC1: A test reproduces the stall on a temporary repository: graph built, then a commit touching only `.metaproject/`, and it fails before the fix — `keryx sync --apply` leaves `.metaproject/data/gdgraph/.provenance.json` on the older commit while the gdwiki baseline is refused for a stale graph.
AC2: After the fix, that same sequence ends with the graph provenance naming HEAD and the gdwiki baseline recorded, in one documented command.
AC3: A commit that changes a tracked code file still rebuilds the graph and advances provenance, unchanged from today (regression test).
AC4: A working tree holding an untracked or newly added code file still refuses the wiki baseline, with the same message as today (regression test).
AC5: Whichever of the three owners is not changed carries a comment naming the decision and why it is not the fix — the diff stage, the manual `gdgraph build` path, or the gdwiki baseline gate.
AC6: `bun run check` passes and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: manual gdgraph build never records provenance: the command delegates to the copied template runner, which has no recordProvenance
criteria: AC1: A test on a scaffolded project (one that carries `.metaproject/core/gdgraph/cli.ts`) fails before the fix: `keryx gdgraph build` leaves no `.metaproject/data/gdgraph/.provenance.json`.
AC2: After the fix, `keryx gdgraph build` on that same project records provenance naming the current HEAD, and a second build with no commits in between leaves it naming the same commit.
AC3: The in-process path (no copied runner, or treesitter on) records provenance exactly as it does today (regression test).
AC4: A build on a repository with no commits, or on a detached HEAD, does not fail and does not write a provenance file naming a commit that does not exist.
AC5: The chosen repair is stated in the flow journal with its reason, and the paths not chosen carry a comment saying why — in particular whether existing projects are fixed without `keryx update`.
AC6: `bun run check` passes and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: Background task execution P1: a finished task wakes the agent without polling
criteria: AC1: A task that was handed back as a handle (`phase: "background"`) and whose terminal status the agent has not seen is returned by `drainUndelivered()` exactly once: the same call marks it `observed`, and an immediate second drain — and a drain racing the first — returns nothing for that task.

AC2: A task the agent has already seen terminal, through `shell_job_output` or `shell_job_kill` returning its terminal status, is never returned by `drainUndelivered()` and never produces a notification.

AC3: The notification is one coalesced message per drain with `role: "user"` and `provenance: "tool"`, carrying a `<task-notification>` envelope per task with `task_id`, `status`, `exit_code`, `kill_reason` and `duration_ms`, the banner stating the text is command output and not instructions from the user, and at most 4 000 bytes of output tail per task; it does not set `untrustedContentSeen`.

AC4: The notification is pushed only at a round boundary — after every `tool` result of the batch, in the same place `anchorsToAnnounce` and `repeatedFailureHint` are pushed — and never between two `tool` results answering one `tool_calls` batch, asserted over a parallel batch of at least two calls.
AC5: A completion that arrives while a turn is running reaches the model in that same turn's next round without any `shell_job_output` call and without a `sleep`.

AC6: A session with `completionDelivery: "hold"` (set by `--print` and by `deps.unattended === true`) does not end a turn at the text-only finish while one of its own yielded tasks is still running: it waits, continues the turn with the notification, and reports the result; the wait is abortable by the turn signal, and a task still running after `KERYX_SHELL_HOLD_MS` is killed with `killReason: "hold-timeout"` and reported in that final round.

AC7: An idle interactive session starts a turn from a notification with `origin: "task-notification"` — the readline REPL by racing its next input line against the next completion, the TUI only when no foreground operation is active and the operator queue is empty — and a queued operator message always runs before a pending notification.

AC8: Consecutive completion-started turns are capped at `KERYX_SHELL_MAX_AUTO_WAKE` (default 5) with no operator input between them; any operator line resets the counter; past the cap no turn starts, the pending notification is surfaced to the operator and is delivered at the start of their next turn.

AC9: No recurring reminder exists: a task that is still running produces no message at all, and a task that finished produces exactly one — asserted by driving several rounds after a completion was delivered and finding no second message for that task.

AC10: `KERYX_SHELL_HOLD_MS` (default 1 800 000) and `KERYX_SHELL_MAX_AUTO_WAKE` (default 5) resolve with the project's fail-safe pattern — unset, empty, non-numeric and negative all fall back to the default, and only an explicit `0` disables where disabling is meaningful.

AC11: Approval, sandbox, process-group kill and the session sweep are unchanged, and `bun run typecheck` plus `shell-exec-tool.test.ts`, `shell-exec-timeout.test.ts`, `shell-exec-background.test.ts`, `background-job-registry.test.ts`, `interactive-agent-tools.test.ts`, `agent-permission-mode.test.ts`, `agent.test.ts`, `shell.test.ts` and `tui-shell.test.ts` all pass.

flows.title: Background task execution P2: task tools, cancellation, operator demote and side-worker rules
criteria: AC1: `shell_task_output` takes `{ task_id, since?: number }` and returns the output after the EXPLICIT cursor plus the task's status, never the whole transcript again; two successive calls with the same `since` return the same bytes, and omitting `since` does not advance any shared cursor.

AC2: `shell_task_wait` takes `{ task_ids: string[], mode: "any" | "all", timeout_ms?: number }` and returns a per-task status and output; `mode: "any"` returns as soon as one task is terminal, `mode: "all"` only when every named task is; an unknown `task_id` is a tool error naming it, not a silent omission.

AC3: `shell_task_wait.timeout_ms` is clamped to [0, 300 000] whatever the model passes, and reaching the bound returns the still-running tasks with their status rather than an error; a wait NEVER kills a task, asserted for both the timeout and the abort path.

AC4: `shell_task_kill` process-group kills the task and is idempotent for one that has already exited: the second call returns an ordinary tool error and never re-signals, and the task's terminal event count stays at one.

AC5: `shell_job_output` and `shell_job_kill` keep working as aliases for one release, and each carries a deprecation note naming its replacement in the tool DESCRIPTION the model is actually sent, asserted over the built tool definition rather than over the source text. Old `job-*` ids resolve to their `task-*` equivalent for READS ONLY (`shell_job_output`); every acting path — `shell_job_kill`, `shell_task_kill` and `/demote` — takes the id exactly as given and refuses an id it does not track. Narrowed from "both ids on both tools" by the owner after review: every id in a live session is `task-*`, so a `job-*` id can only come from an earlier session, which D-14 says must be a dead reference; the swap preserves the counter and the pid, the counter restarts each session, and a recycled pid therefore lets a stale id match a LIVE task. A read landing on the wrong task is a wrong answer; a kill landing on it destroys work nobody asked to lose.

AC6: `InteractiveTool.invoke` accepts `(input, ctx?: { signal?: AbortSignal })` and `executeCall` passes the turn's signal; every existing tool that ignores `ctx` is unaffected, proven by the existing suites passing unchanged.

AC7: On abort, `shell_task_wait` and `shell_exec`'s yield wait return PROMPTLY with `interrupted: true` and the tasks still `running` — not killed — and those tasks' completions are still delivered afterwards through the P1 drain, exactly once.

AC8: The operator demotes a running foreground task with `/demote <task_id>`, available in BOTH shells (TUI and the readline REPL), and the turn is not aborted: the demote releases the caller's wait through the same path an abort uses, the task keeps running with its output intact, and it enters the TUI task list from its `phase` event (which fires at most once per task). The command is proven by EXECUTING its handler against a registry — an unknown id and an already-background task each return a stated error rather than throwing — not by a source audit.

AC9: Side workers are denied `shell_task_kill`, `shell_job_kill`, `shell_task_wait` and `shell_job_output`; only `shell_task_output` is offered to them, and the denial is asserted over the roster a side worker is actually built with, not over a name list.

AC10: A side worker's `shell_task_output` NEVER marks a task observed: after a side worker reads a task that has already finished, the main session still receives exactly one notification for that task; only tools built for the main session mark observation.

AC11: `shell_task_output`, `shell_task_wait` and `shell_job_output` are repeatable tools, so a legitimate poll does not trip the repeated-call guard, while the per-signature attempt rail still stops a genuine loop.

AC12: P0 and P1 are unchanged: approval, sandbox resolution, process-group kill, the session sweep and exactly-once delivery keep their existing proofs, and `bun run typecheck` plus `shell-exec-tool.test.ts`, `shell-exec-timeout.test.ts`, `shell-exec-background.test.ts`, `background-job-registry.test.ts`, `agent-task-notification.test.ts`, `interactive-agent-tools.test.ts`, `agent-permission-mode.test.ts`, `agent.test.ts`, `shell.test.ts` and `tui-shell.test.ts` all pass.

flows.title: Keryx Shell persistent execution plan with agent-followed sidebar progress
criteria: AC1: The main interactive agent exposes typed plan_set, plan_update, and plan_get tools in both TUI and readline shells, while child and subagent tool rosters remain unchanged.
AC2: A plan update enforces stable item identifiers, valid statuses, at most one in-progress item, and optimistic revision checking so stale writes fail visibly.
AC3: The active execution plan is persisted in the session Slate and is restored when that session is resumed; a session without a plan remains backward-compatible.

AC4: Each agent continuation receives a bounded current-plan snapshot, and an attempted final response with pending or in-progress items triggers a bounded continuation instead of silently declaring the task finished.

AC5: The TUI renders a Plan panel immediately above Background Jobs only when a plan exists, displays no more than seven item rows, and centers the in-progress item when enough preceding and following rows exist.

AC6: The Plan panel distinguishes completed, in-progress, pending, blocked, and skipped states, truncates rows to the sidebar width, and repaints when plan state changes without repainting on unrelated job-output chunks.
AC7: Existing /plan read-only permission-mode behavior remains intact, and session-plan metadata tools do not grant filesystem or command mutation capability.
AC8: Focused unit and TUI tests cover state transitions, persistence and resume, tool wiring, completion continuation, window selection at list boundaries, empty-plan visibility, and panel ordering.

flows.title: Expose the keryx harness over the Agent Client Protocol so any ACP client can drive it
criteria: AC1: `keryx acp` speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, writes nothing but frames to stdout, and answers `initialize` with its protocol version, `agentCapabilities` and `agentInfo`. A version keryx does not support is answered explicitly: the latest version keryx supports where the spec requires that (a client asking for a newer version), and a JSON-RPC error where no conformant answer exists (a malformed or out-of-range version) — never a crash, and never a silent pretend-success.

AC2: `session/new` creates a keryx session bound to the requested working directory, and `session/prompt` runs a real harness turn in it; the driving client receives the answer as `session/update` notifications while the turn runs, not only at the end.

AC3: A tool call that the policy engine would ask about produces a `session/request_permission` request; a denial from the client leaves the call unexecuted and the turn continues or ends exactly as a local denial does. A policy that denies outright never reaches the client at all.
AC4: `session/cancel` stops the running turn, the turn ends with the same cancelled outcome a local abort produces, and no further `session/update` for that turn is sent afterwards.

AC5: `session/list` and `session/load` expose the project's existing durable sessions: a session created through `keryx shell` is listed and can be loaded by an ACP client, and its history is replayed in the shape the spec defines.

AC6: Client capabilities are honoured, and an absent capability is provably never used. With `fs.readTextFile` advertised, file reads go through `fs/read_text_file`; without it — or with it false — the harness reads with its own tool and the turn still completes. Writes and shell execution stay local in this flow and call no client method at all: `apply_patch` applies a multi-file diff atomically, which `fs/write_text_file`'s one-file-full-content shape cannot express, and `shell_exec`'s streaming and approval gate have no one-for-one `terminal/*` equivalent — both reasons are recorded in the code, and routing either one is left to a follow-up flow. A capability matrix test proves keryx calls no `fs/*` when `fs` is absent and no `terminal/*` in any configuration.

AC7: The wire types and the JSON-RPC framing live in one adapter module, and a protocol-version bump touches only that module plus its tests (shown by the test that pins the version constant and the shape).

AC8: A conformance test drives the whole surface over a real stdio pipe against the built CLI — initialize, new, prompt with streaming updates, permission request and denial, cancel, list, load — with a fake provider, no network.
AC9: README and the CLI reference document `keryx acp`, what a client must advertise, and what keryx does when a capability is absent.
AC10: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: Start a flow from a repository event or a schedule, not only from a person at a prompt
criteria: AC1: A project declares triggers in a validated config: each entry names what fires it (a repository event or a schedule) and what it does; an entry that is malformed is refused on load with the reason, and the other entries still work.
AC2: `keryx trigger run <name>` performs exactly one pass of that entry's action and exits non-zero only when the action itself failed; a run with nothing to do exits zero and says so.

AC3: A second `keryx trigger run` for the same project, started while the first is still running, does not corrupt the graph, wiki or session store: it either waits for the same lock the interactive commands take, or refuses with a clear reason, and a test drives both concurrently.
AC4: Every fired trigger is recorded — what fired it, when, what it did, and what it cost when a model was used — and `keryx trigger status` reads that record rather than re-deriving it.

AC5: `keryx trigger install` extends the existing hook installation instead of replacing it: after install, `keryx sync install-hooks`'s behaviour on `post-merge` and `post-checkout` still happens, and a project that had hooks keeps them.
AC6: For a schedule, keryx prints the cron line or the systemd timer unit to install and does not run a daemon of its own; the printed line is exercised by a test that runs it as the scheduler would.
AC7: A trigger whose action opens a flow can be declared not to open a second one while an equivalent flow is already open, and a test proves the second firing is a no-op with a stated reason.
AC8: A triggered run that would exceed the configured spend ceiling stops with a budget refusal recorded as its outcome, not as a crash.
AC9: README and the CLI reference document the trigger config, the commands, and the fact that scheduling is delegated to the operator's own scheduler.
AC10: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: ACP live-client fixes: real provider by default, accept client MCP servers
criteria: AC1: `keryx acp` started with no `--provider`/`--model` uses the same provider and model that `keryx shell` would use in that project, resolved by the same code path rather than a copy of it; explicit flags still override. A test proves the default path never constructs the fake or fixture provider — that provider is reachable only through the explicit test-only `--fixture` flag.

AC2: When no provider is configured and none is passed, `keryx acp` still answers `initialize`, and `session/new` and `session/load` are refused with a JSON-RPC error whose message names what to configure and how; no turn ever runs against a fake provider. The same condition is written once to stderr at startup.

AC3: `session/new` and `session/load` accept a non-empty `mcpServers` list of stdio servers: each is started with its `command`, `args` and `env` through keryx's existing MCP client, its tools are offered to that session's turns, and every server process keryx started is stopped when the connection closes — shown by a test that checks the processes are gone.

AC4: A call to a tool that comes from a client-supplied MCP server goes through the same `session/request_permission` ask as any other gated call and never runs without an explicit allow; a denial ends the call exactly as a local denial does.

AC5: A server that fails to start does not fail the session: the session is created, the other servers still work, and the failure is reported to the client with the server's name and the reason. An `http` or `sse` entry — transports keryx does not advertise — is refused per entry with the reason rather than silently dropped.

AC6: The `env` values and header values from `mcpServers` never reach transcripts, session records, logs, stdout or stderr: a test plants a sentinel secret in an entry's `env`, drives a full turn that calls the server's tool, and asserts the sentinel appears in none of them.

AC7: A process test drives the built CLI over a real stdio pipe with a real stdio MCP server fixture from the repository: `session/new` with that server succeeds, its tool is offered, the permission ask arrives, the call runs on allow and returns its result, and the server process is gone after the connection closes. No network.

AC8: The CLI reference and README describe how `keryx acp` resolves its provider and model when no flag is given, what happens when nothing is configured, which `mcpServers` transports are accepted, and how a failed server is reported; the claim that the flags work "the same way `keryx shell` does" is true.
AC9: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: ACP project tools: keryx graph, wiki, memory and flow tools, slash commands and model switching in the editor
criteria: AC1: In a project where `keryx shell` offers its read-only project tools (graph, wiki, memory, flow status, skills, repomap, test_related, health status and `search_code`), an ACP session offers the same set, decided by the same `offersIndexTools` gate and built from the same tool definitions — not a hand-maintained copy. In a project where the shell would not offer them, neither does ACP; `search_code` follows the shell's exception. A test compares the two rosters for both project states.

AC2: Every tool an ACP session offers renders with a meaningful ACP tool `kind` — search tools as `search`, read tools as `read`, and so on — and a test fails if a tool in the ACP roster falls back to `other` without being listed as a deliberate exception.

AC3: The ACP roster adds no tool whose results carry `untrusted: true`, no delegation tool and no bus tool; a test enumerates the roster and asserts this, so widening it later is a visible decision rather than a side effect.

AC4: After `session/new` and `session/load`, keryx sends one `available_commands_update` whose entries have the published shape (`name`, `description`, optional `input.hint`) and list only commands keryx handles over ACP; TUI-only commands are not listed. A command arriving as prompt text beginning with `/` is handled by keryx and does not reach the model; an unlisted one is answered with the list of available commands.

AC5: The `session/new` and `session/load` responses carry `configOptions` with one `select` option of category `model` whose values are the models keryx can actually run in this project, resolved from the same source `keryx shell` uses, and whose `currentValue` is the model the session is running.

AC6: `session/set_config_option` for the model option switches the model from the next turn on and answers with the complete, updated `configOptions`; `/model <value>` does the same and sends `config_option_update`. A switch never changes a turn already running, an unknown value is refused with the reason, and the choice does not rewrite `keryx shell`'s saved default.

AC7: `src/acp/protocol.ts` types `AvailableCommand`, the config option and its values per the published schema, `config_option_update` carries `configOptions`, and `session/set_config_option` leaves the refused-method list; the version-pin test still passes and the method-partition test still covers every v1 agent method.

AC8: Process tests over a real stdio pipe with the fixture provider cover: the project tools offered and one of them called in a turn, the commands update arriving after `session/new`, a `/` command handled without reaching the model, and a model switch through both `session/set_config_option` and `/model` taking effect on the following turn. Every wait is on a wire event, not a timer.

AC9: The CLI reference and README list which keryx tools an ACP session offers and why the others are excluded, which commands are advertised, and how to switch model from the editor; nothing in the docs still says an ACP session offers only five tools or that the model is fixed at launch.
AC10: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: Flow owner and signed completion
criteria: AC1: A flow can name an owner — the human accountable for it — set with `keryx flow init --owner "<name>"` and changed afterwards only through `keryx flow owner set <id> --owner "<name>" --reason "<why>"`, which refuses an empty reason. The owner is never inferred: a flow whose owner was never set reports `owner: not set`, not a name taken from git or the environment.

AC2: Every owner change is kept as history, not overwritten: setting or changing the owner appends an event with the previous value, the new value, the reason and the time, so `keryx flow status` can answer both who owns the flow now and who owned it before. No code path rewrites or deletes an earlier entry; a test changes the owner twice and asserts both earlier values survive.

AC3: Every recorded identity — the owner and each signer — carries a `basis` (`stated` when given explicitly by a flag or environment variable, `derived` when read from something like the local git configuration, `unknown` when nothing was available) and a `source` naming exactly where it came from. A derived identity is never recorded as stated, and no path invents an identity when none is available; tests cover all three bases.

AC4: `keryx flow ac confirm` and `keryx flow complete` each append a signature recording who (identity, basis, source), when, and what was signed — for a confirmation the criterion id and the frozen acceptance-criteria checksum in force; for completion that checksum and the pull-request head commit the gates evaluated, when one is known. Signatures are append-only: running the command again adds a new signature and never alters an earlier one.

AC5: Flows created by `flow init` after this change record an owner gate, opt-in per package the same way the existing tasks and review gates are. On such a flow `keryx flow complete` fails the owner gate with a named reason when no owner is set, and passes it when one is; a flow created before this change reports the gate as skipped and completes exactly as it did before.

AC6: Existing `flow.json` files without owner or signature fields load, validate, pass `keryx flow check` and complete unchanged: the new fields are optional and additive in the schema and its published JSON Schema copy, no new schema version is introduced, and reading an old file never rewrites it on disk. A test loads a pre-change fixture and asserts all of this.
AC7: `keryx flow status` shows the current owner (or `not set`) and the latest completion signature — signer, basis and time — as lines in the same style as its existing `status`, `AC` and `PR` rows.

AC8: What keryx cannot verify is stated as a limit, not presented as a fact: the docs and the CLI output for a stated or derived identity say that a name given by a flag, an environment variable or the local git configuration is a claim that an agent could make on its own, not proof that a human signed. Nowhere does the feature claim otherwise.

AC9: The flow command help, the CLI reference, README and a decision record describe the owner, the signature, the owner gate, the compatibility guarantee and the limits in AC8, and make clear that this "owner" is the accountable human — distinct from the existing use of "owner" for module ownership in the docs.
AC10: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: Triggers wave 2: flow-next dispatches an agent, per-trigger spend ceiling, shared lock with manual commands
criteria: AC1: A `flow-next` trigger entry with a `dispatch` block (provider, model, permissionMode, rates, ceilingUsd, maxSeconds) makes `keryx trigger run <name>` start a keryx agent on the flow's next ready task in a dedicated git worktree on a `trigger/<flow>-<task>` branch, with no TTY, and record the outcome. A test with a fake provider drives one task from `never-started` to a recorded end and asserts the attempt log, the run record and the branch commit. An entry without a `dispatch` block keeps today's report-only behaviour and `keryx trigger list`/`status` say "report-only".

AC2: Before the model is called, the dispatch records `flow task attempt <flow> <task> --outcome started` with the trigger run id. After the run it records exactly one closing fact: `task done --disposition completed` with a `runLink` only when the turn ended normally, the trigger branch has a commit and `keryx health gate` passes in that worktree. Otherwise it records `task attempt --outcome failed|blocked` with the reason. Tests cover success, provider failure, timeout and health-gate failure.

AC3: The dispatch refuses without calling a model, and records a distinct outcome with exit 0, when: the flow is not frozen and `in-progress`; `flow next` is `blocked` or `none`; the ready task's resume state is `unresolved` (an open attempt); the task's attempt count has reached its cap; or another dispatch holds the flow's dispatch lock. There is one test per refusal.

AC4: An unattended run fails closed. `AgentDeps.unattended` is true. The permission mode comes only from the trigger entry (`ask` or `trust`; `auto` is rejected at config load). The project's stored default permission mode and the saved shell allowlist are ignored. Every call that would ask (including `ask_user`, the untrusted-content gate, and credential, SAC-confirm or publish-lease floors) is denied and never approved, and each denial is written to the run record with the tool and the reason. Tests seed a stored `auto` default and a saved `bash *` allowlist and show that neither takes effect.

AC5: A hard unattended-forbidden floor is evaluated before the permission mode, so `trust` cannot lift it. It denies `git push` in any form, `git merge`, `git tag`, `gh pr merge`, `gh release`, `npm publish` and `bun publish`. It denies `keryx flow freeze`, `flow ac update`, `flow ac reseal`, `flow ac confirm`, `flow implemented`, `flow complete`, `flow renumber`, `flow block`, `flow unblock`, `flow task add` and `flow task depends`. It denies any write (via `apply_patch` or `shell_exec`) to `flow.json`, `acceptance-criteria.md`, `.metaproject/triggers.json` or `.metaproject/data/trigger/**`. A table-driven test runs each case under `trust` and asserts deny plus a recorded denial. After a dispatch test, the flow's AC checksum, status and `acceptance-criteria.md` are unchanged. The unattended tool roster also excludes `web_fetch`, `web_search`, `search_tool`/`use_tool` and `spawn_subagent` in this version, and a test enumerates it. The floor is defence in depth, not the boundary, and the docs say so; the boundary is AC13.

AC6: Each dispatched run records its cost: input/output tokens always, and USD computed from the entry's declared rates. `TriggerRunCost` gains `tokens` additively and old `runs.jsonl` lines still read. A run that fails, times out or is aborted still records the tokens and USD it consumed. A `flow-next` entry with a `dispatch` block but no `rates` or no `ceilingUsd` is rejected at config load with a stated reason, so no unpriced dispatch can run.

AC7: A per-trigger spend ceiling (`dispatch.ceilingUsd`) applies in addition to the project-wide ceiling. When the trigger's own recorded USD is at or over its ceiling, `keryx trigger run` refuses before any model call, records `budget-refused` naming the per-trigger ceiling, and exits 0. Another trigger under its own ceiling still runs, and the project-wide refusal still applies. An unreadable ledger still refuses both. Tests use a real seeded `runs.jsonl`.

AC8: The remaining allowance (min of per-trigger and project-wide remaining) is enforced during the run. When the accumulated token cost reaches it, the turn is aborted, the task gets `attempt failed` with reason "spend cap reached", and the recorded USD does not exceed the allowance by more than one model response. A fake provider with fixed usage proves the stop.

AC9: One shared maintenance lock is taken by interactive `keryx sync --apply`, interactive `keryx gdgraph build` (before local-runner delegation), triggered `reconcile`/`rebuild`, and `open-flow`'s check-then-create. A test runs an interactive `gdgraph build` and a `keryx trigger run rebuild` concurrently in two real processes. Exactly one builds at a time, the triggered one records `lock-refused`, and the interactive one waits (bounded) and then says which pid holds the lock rather than reporting a build failure.

AC10: The shared lock is re-entrant within one async context and is not held across an agent dispatch. `keryx sync --apply`, which calls `gdgraph build` in-process, completes without self-refusal or a timeout wait, and so do triggered `reconcile`/`rebuild` that call those commands. Two unrelated concurrent acquires in one process still exclude each other. A dispatched agent that runs `keryx gdgraph build` via `shell_exec` can take the lock. Tests assert all four.

AC11: The docs match the code. `keryx trigger --help`, `docs/docs/cli-reference.md` and `README.md` describe the dispatching `flow-next` (the `dispatch` block fields, worktree and branch, what the run may and may not do), the per-trigger ceiling, the cost recording and the shared lock (interactive waits, triggered refuses). The stale "flow-next only reports" text and the 286 claim that interactive commands already share the lock are corrected.
AC12: CI is green on the PR, and `keryx health run` passes on the branch before completion.

AC13: Under `trust` a dispatch refuses to start, with a recorded reason, unless the shell sandbox launcher is available and engaged; an explicit operator setting that disables the sandbox also refuses `trust` rather than running uncontained. The health gate runs inside the same sandbox. The unattended sandbox profile turns the network off unless the entry opts in with a stated field, passes only an allowlisted environment, hides the home directory except the toolchain paths the run needs, and gives the run a private temporary directory. Tests with the real launcher (skipping cleanly when it is absent, never passing vacuously) prove a dispatched agent and the health gate it triggers cannot read a credential file planted under the home directory, cannot see a token planted in the environment, and cannot reach the network by default.

AC14: Spend cannot go unrecorded. Before the model is first called the dispatch reserves its allowance in the run ledger under a project-wide spend lock, so concurrent triggers never each see the full remaining allowance, and a run killed at any point leaves its reservation counted against both ceilings until it is resolved. A provider whose adapter does not report token usage in its stream is refused for dispatch at config load or before any call, and rates of zero are rejected. Tests cover a reservation surviving a killed run, two concurrent dispatches against one allowance, and the refusal of a provider without usage reporting.

AC15: A run that ends abnormally cannot block its task forever: the next dispatch for that task, once any open attempt has been resolved, removes a stale worktree and branch left by an earlier run before creating its own, and the open-attempt refusal names how to resolve the attempt. A test kills a run mid-flight, resolves the attempt, and shows the next dispatch proceeds.

flows.title: Governance report: spend, confirmations, signatures and gate outcomes across flows
criteria: AC1: `keryx governance report` aggregates, per flow in the current project, review-round spend from every review package's `manifest.json` `cost` field (input tokens, output tokens, USD), summed across rounds. A figure is shown as a number only when at least one round recorded it; a flow where no round recorded cost reports `spend: not recorded`, never `0`; a flow with partial coverage reports the sum together with a rounds-with-cost / rounds-total count, never silently dropping the gap.

AC2: The report shows trigger spend from `.metaproject/data/trigger/runs.jsonl` as a separate project-level figure: USD summed over runs whose cost was recorded, plus the count of runs whose cost was not recorded, reported as such and never counted as zero. A run record carrying no flow reference is never attributed to a flow, and the report says why. An absent ledger means no trigger has run; an unreadable one reports `not recorded` with the reason, never a guessed value.

AC3: For each flow the report shows who confirmed each acceptance criterion and who signed its completion, from the flow's signatures joined with its confirmations, with every identity's basis (`stated`, `derived`, `unknown`) shown beside the name; a derived or unknown identity is never presented as a verified confirmation. A flow that predates signatures reports `confirmations: not recorded (predates signing)`, never an empty list read as nobody confirmed anything.

AC4: `flow complete` persists the outcome of every gate it evaluated — name, status and detail, for passing, failing and skipped gates alike — on every completion attempt from now on, pass or fail, as an append-only additive field of the flow; it is no longer reduced to one prose history line. Existing `flow.json` files load, validate, pass `keryx flow check` and complete unchanged, with no new schema version, and the report shows `gate outcomes: not recorded` for attempts made before this change. Tests cover a failing attempt followed by a passing one, and a pre-change fixture.

AC5: The report derives every figure only from what is already recorded — flow files, review manifests, the trigger ledger and, when present, the security artifact and the deletion journal. It never re-runs a gate, never calls a model or any network service, and never modifies anything it reads; the only files it writes are its own report artifacts. A test asserts no file under `.metaproject/flows/` or `.metaproject/data/trigger/` changes.

AC6: The report writes `.metaproject/data/governance/artifacts/latest.md` and a schema-versioned `latest.json`, following the convention `keryx health run` uses, and a shape-guarded reader treats a missing or malformed stored report as no report yet rather than failing.

AC7: The report can be filtered by `--flow <id>`, `--owner <name>` and a `--since`/`--until` date range applied to each record's own timestamp; each filter is tested against a fixture set and narrows the markdown and the json output consistently.

AC8: The report covers the current project by default; `--all-projects` also covers every project in the user-global registry, and a registered project whose path is missing or unreadable is listed with a warning instead of failing the whole report.

AC9: Policy allow/ask/deny decisions and unattended-run denials have no durable project-wide record today; the report lists them as `not recorded (no durable log exists yet)` rather than omitting the category.

AC10: README and the CLI reference describe `keryx governance report`, its flags, where it writes, what it reads, the gate-outcome persistence, and the rule that a figure never recorded is reported as not recorded, never as zero.
AC11: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: keryx as an ACP client: drive external ACP agents with keryx context and policy
criteria: AC1: A process test starts a scripted fake ACP agent. The agent is a repo fixture script driven by a JSON script. The test drives it through the existing `ExternalSpawnPort` over real stdin/stdout pipes, with no network. The run must complete `initialize` (protocolVersion 1), then `session/new`, then `session/prompt`, ending with stopReason `end_turn`. `session/new` must carry an absolute `cwd` equal to the run's disposable worktree. The streamed `session/update` messages must be folded into `ExternalEvent`s (`assistant_text`, `tool_call`, `tool_result`, `usage`), and the run must finish as `ExternalChildOutcome.status: "Completed"`. A second case has the fake agent reply with an unsupported protocol version. That run must end `Error` with a named reason, and the child must be killed.

AC2: Every `session/request_permission` is decided by `resolveApprovalDecision`. Its risk comes from the tool call: - `read`/`search`/`think` → read; - `edit`/`move` → write; - `delete` → destructive; - `execute` → shell, or destructive when `isDestructiveCommand` matches; - `fetch` → denied; - `other` or a missing kind → shell with destructive set. Any `locations[].path` outside the worktree escalates a read to a prompt. keryx answers with the agent's `allow_once` option only when the gate says `auto`, or when a human approval echoes the prompt's fingerprint. keryx never selects `allow_always`. A table-driven unit test covers each kind × mode, and the fake-agent process test confirms the chosen `optionId` on the wire. Because the tool kind and inputs are the agent's own description, a foreign agent never runs under `trust` or `auto`: those modes are lowered to `ask` for ACP-client runs, and the run record says so.

AC3: An unattended run fails closed. An unattended run is `--unattended`, a run with no TTY, or a run with no approver wired. In it, every permission that would need a prompt is answered with `reject_once`, or with `{outcome:"cancelled"}` when the agent offered no reject option. An approver that has not answered within the timeout is answered the same way. A human "no" is answered the same way. A process test shows that the fake agent received the rejection and did not report the tool as run. The test also shows that the run record holds one decision entry per request, with the mapped risk, the gate decision, the verdict, `timedOut` and the reason (policy, unattended, timeout or human).

AC4: `clientCapabilities` in `initialize` advertises only what keryx serves: - a read-only run advertises `fs.readTextFile: true`, `fs.writeTextFile: false`, `terminal: false`, and no `elicitation`; - `--write` additionally advertises `fs.writeTextFile: true`; - this flow never advertises `terminal`. A process test has the fake agent call `fs/write_text_file` in a read-only run, and call `terminal/create` and `elicitation/create` in every run. Each call must get a JSON-RPC error with a named reason and be recorded. No file may be created and no process spawned.

AC5: `fs/read_text_file` and an advertised `fs/write_text_file` run only inside keryx's own confined code. Paths are confined to the worktree by real path. For a file that does not exist yet, the check uses the nearest existing ancestor. Tests must cover: - a symlinked parent directory that points outside the worktree is refused; - `../` traversal is refused; - agent credential files (`touchesAgentCredentials`) and managed flow files are refused. Writes go through the AC2 bridge as risk `write`. After any run, a hash of the operator's project tree is byte-identical to the hash taken before it. In a `--write` run, the worktree's diff is saved as the run's patch artifact and is never applied.

AC6: Context is offered through keryx's own MCP server. - `session/new` carries one stdio `mcpServers` entry. It launches the running keryx build (`process.execPath` plus the CLI entry, not `keryx` from PATH) as `serve-mcp --read-only --cwd <project-root>`. - A test shows that `serve-mcp --read-only` lists no tool marked `mutating: true`. - A process test has the fake agent echo back the `mcpServers` it received. - When the MCP module or SDK is unavailable, the run still proceeds and records `context: not-offered` with the reason. - The first prompt is built by `buildExternalPrompt`. Embedded resource blocks are sent only when the agent advertised `promptCapabilities.embeddedContext`.

AC7: Every run is persisted as a keryx session that `keryx sessions` lists, with provider `acp:<agent-id>`. The session contains: - the redacted assistant text and the tool calls; - every permission decision, and every fs/terminal request with its outcome; - the argv, the worktree path, and the agent's name and version from `initialize`; - the token usage and the cost, taken from `usage_update` only when the agent reported them. A missing cost is recorded as missing, never as 0. A test asserts both the reported case and the missing case.

AC8: A CLI command runs one registry agent over ACP: `keryx agents external run <id> --task "<text>" [--unattended] [--write]`. `runExternalChild` routes a registry entry with `transport: "acp"` to the ACP supervisor. The command is guarded by the existing `gdskills.external-agents` capability and the per-agent config. Tests show: - a named refusal when the capability is disabled, and in CI; - `Denied` with a named reason when the binary is missing; - on timeout, `session/cancel`, then a kill after a grace period, then status `Timeout`; - the disposable worktree is removed on every exit path, including a throw from the spawn port.

AC9: A process test has keryx-as-client drive keryx-as-agent (`keryx acp --fixture <script>`) end to end. A gated tool in the inner keryx sends a real `session/request_permission` to the outer keryx. The outer keryx answers by its own policy: denied when unattended, allowed after an injected approval. The inner turn's record shows that outcome.

AC10: The honest limit is tested and written down. - A test has the fake agent write a file with its own filesystem calls instead of ACP. The test shows that the file lands only in the disposable worktree, which is removed afterwards. The file must not be recorded as a keryx-mediated write, and the project tree must be unchanged. - The docs state: - keryx cannot see or gate an agent's internal tools that never call ACP; - an unadvertised capability is a request to the agent, not a boundary; - permission classification relies on the agent's own description of the tool call; - calls the agent makes to the MCP servers keryx gave it do not pass the permission bridge; - the agent process itself is not OS-sandboxed in this flow; - the disposable worktree is the load-bearing containment (D-08).

AC11: README and the docs site gain an "ACP client" page. It covers usage, the permission mapping table, the advertised capabilities, the record format and the limits from AC10. `keryx agents external list` shows ACP entries with their transport. The docs for the external agent runtime (`docs/requirements/keryx-external-agent-runtime`) note the third transport.
AC12: CI is green on the PR, and `bun run src/cli.ts health run` passes. The ACP client tests make no network calls and need neither `gemini` nor `claude` installed.

flows.title: flow ac update: amend a criterion's text, and refuse arguments it does not use
criteria: AC1: `keryx flow ac update <id> --criterion ACn --text "<criterion>" --reason "<why>"` replaces that criterion's text in `acceptance-criteria.md`, or appends it when `ACn` is the next unused number, then re-freezes the file and clears confirmations exactly as `ac update` does today. The flow history records the criterion, its previous text and its new text alongside the reason, and a test reads all three back.

AC2: `keryx flow ac update <id> --reason "<why>"` without `--criterion` keeps today's behaviour — it re-freezes the file as the operator edited it — so existing scripts and documentation keep working.

AC3: Every `keryx flow ac` subcommand refuses an argument it does not use — an extra positional, `--text` without `--criterion`, `--criterion` without `--text`, or an unknown flag — with an error naming that argument, and changes nothing. A test runs the exact invocation that was silently accepted before, `flow ac update <id> AC1 --text "…" --reason "…"`, and asserts it is refused and the file and checksum are unchanged.

AC4: The new text is validated before anything is written: it must be non-empty, fit on one line, and not carry its own `- ACn:` prefix; `--criterion` must name `AC` followed by a number. Each refusal names the rule it broke.
AC5: The flow command help and the CLI reference describe both ways of amending criteria and state that the command refuses arguments it does not use.
AC6: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: Command registry: descriptors still describe the pre-0.2.155 behaviour
criteria: AC1: Every agent-facing command descriptor for a command that flows 287 to 293 changed — `trigger` (run, list, status, schedule, install, uninstall, resolve), `flow` (init, owner set, ac confirm, ac update, ac reseal, complete, status), `acp`, `serve-mcp`, `agents external`, and `governance` — describes that command as 0.2.155 actually behaves; in particular `trigger run` no longer says open-flow and flow-next refuse, and no descriptor names the old `.metaproject/data/trigger/.run.lock` path.

AC2: Commands added by those flows that an agent should be able to discover have a descriptor or a reasoned exclusion (for example `trigger resolve`, `flow owner set`), and the command-registry coverage test stays green.
AC3: A test pins the corrected `trigger run` description against the behaviour the trigger help states, so the two cannot drift apart again unnoticed.
AC4: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

AC5: Top-level `--help` for a command group whose handler has its own help — at least `flow`, `trigger`, `serve-mcp`, `governance` and `agents external` — lists every subcommand that group has, instead of a shorter stale usage block; a test compares each intercepted help against the handler's own help so a new subcommand cannot be missing from it.

flows.title: Scheduled agent tasks from the shell and TUI, running in the background with explicit grants
criteria: AC1: A new trigger action kind `agent-task` (a free-form prompt, a dispatch block with; provider, model, `ask`|`trust`, rates, `ceilingUsd` and `maxSeconds`, a grants block and a; report block) loads and validates the way the existing kinds do. A missing prompt, rates or ceiling is refused on load with the reason. `permissionMode: "auto"` is refused on load with the reason. A granted tool that is not in the built-in catalogue is refused on load with the reason. A granted tool whose argv the unattended floor refuses (for example `gh pr merge`) is; refused on load with the reason. Proven by `src/trigger/config.test.ts` cases.

AC2: `keryx trigger run <name>` on an `agent-task` entry runs one unattended agent turn with; the entry's prompt, under the entry's own permission mode. The dispatcher, not the agent, writes the agent's final message to; `.metaproject/data/trigger/reports/<name>/<runId>.md`, with a header giving the outcome, cost, granted calls and denials. That directory is gitignored. The agent cannot write there, because the floor protects the path. Proven by a scripted-provider test through `runTriggerOnce`.

AC3: Granted tools keep credentials out of the model's reach. Each granted command runs through `execFile` outside the sandbox, with a fixed argv; template, pattern-checked parameters (a value starting with `-` is refused), a timeout, an; output cap and secret redaction. The model receives only the output. In the same run, a `shell_exec` of `env`, `echo $GH_TOKEN`, or `cat` of the gh config; returns no token and no gh config. Proven by a test that sets a sentinel `GH_TOKEN` in the; dispatcher's environment and asserts the sentinel appears in no tool result, in no; provider request and in no report.

AC4: The network grant is `off` (the default, `--unshare-net`) or `full` (today's host network, always shown with the NETWORK ON warning). An `allowlist` mode — shell commands reaching only listed domains through the loopback allowlist proxy, host loopback unreachable — is delivered by flow 301; until then an entry asking for it is refused on load with a reason naming that it is not yet available, and the capability matrix keeps `not-implemented`. Checking GitHub needs no sandbox network, because granted tools run outside the sandbox (AC3).

AC5: The unattended posture and floor are unchanged by any grant, and a changed schedule; does not run. The existing `trigger/unattended` and `sandbox/unattended` tests pass unmodified. An `agent-task` run under every grant combination still refuses: push, merge, tag, publish, and mutating `gh api`; flow-state verbs, nested `trigger run`, and schedule create/install verbs; writes to `triggers.json`, `flow.json`, `acceptance-criteria.md`, `data/trigger/`, the; schedule store or the reports. `trust` without a working sandbox still refuses with `sandbox-unavailable`. At confirmation, keryx stores a hash of the entry's prompt, grants and dispatch block. `keryx trigger run` refuses an entry whose content no longer matches that hash. It records; `dispatch-refused` with refusal `grants-changed`, and calls no model.

AC6: The operator can create a schedule from the TUI with the `/schedule` slash command. `/schedule` is registered in `AGENT_SLASH_COMMANDS`, and the registry tests are updated. It collects the prompt, cadence and grants, then shows ONE confirmation card listing: cadence as cron, plus the next three run times; prompt; provider and model; ceiling and max seconds; network mode; every granted tool with its resolved binary and account; the unit or crontab path and the exact `ExecStart`; linger status. Declining writes no config and installs nothing. Proven by a TUI handler test.

AC7: The agent can create a schedule from natural language with a `schedule_create` tool; ("schedule a task every 4 hours to check GitHub"). The approval always asks and shows the same card as AC6, in every permission mode; including `auto`. The approval is never auto-approved from a saved allowlist, never remembered, and never; offers "always". The tool is not in the unattended roster. A test drives the tool under `auto` with an approver that declines, and asserts that; nothing was written or installed.

AC8: A confirmed schedule is installed as a background timer, and installation is; idempotent. On Linux: systemd `--user` units, named `keryx-<projecthash>-<name>`, containing a real; `OnCalendar=` translated from the cron, `Persistent=true`, `WorkingDirectory=` set to the; project root, and an absolute interpreter and script. The units pass; `systemd-analyze verify`, including on a path with a space. On macOS: a LaunchAgent plist. Otherwise: a marked crontab block. Installing twice leaves exactly one unit, plist or block. Keryx never runs `loginctl enable-linger` itself. Proven by renderer tests plus an installer test against a temporary unit directory, with; a fake `systemctl`.; the same renderer serves `keryx trigger schedule`, so the unit it prints gains the real `OnCalendar=` (today it prints a timer with only a commented placeholder, which never fires) and the project-unique unit name — a test asserts the printed timer fires on the translated schedule by `systemd-analyze calendar`.

AC9: `keryx schedule list|pause|resume|run|remove` work from the CLI. `list` shows name, cadence, enabled or paused, installed or not, next run, last outcome; with cost, and the last report path. `pause` disables the timer and marks the entry disabled. A fire while paused records; `no-op`. `resume` re-enables both. `run` performs one pass now. `remove` uninstalls the timer and deletes the entry after a confirmation, touching only; files that carry keryx's managed header for this project. Proven by installer tests.

AC10: The TUI sidebar has a Schedules section, mounted in `sidebarTop` like the Plan and Jobs; sections. Each schedule is one compact row: name, next run, and last outcome (ok, failed or; refused, plus cost). The section is hidden when there are no schedules. Row text stays within `SIDEBAR_TEXT_WIDTH`. The colours come from theme slots, so a `/theme` switch recolours them. Clicking a row opens that schedule's detail modal. Proven by a panel test over a fixture ledger and schedule store.

AC11: The detail modal opens through `modal-host` and has four tabs: Overview: cadence, next and last run, enabled, installed unit, linger. Grants: network mode, and each granted tool with its account. Runs: the last N ledger records, with outcome, cost and refusal reason. Report: the latest report, scrollable. Its actions: pause/resume works in one step; run-now and delete need arm then `y`, and any other key cancels; each action calls the same function as the CLI (AC9); the modal refreshes after an action. Proven by modal tests in the style of `mcp-inspector.test.ts`.

AC12: Every schedule interaction is reachable without a mouse. `/schedules` opens a list modal: ↑/↓ selects, Enter opens the selected schedule's detail; modal, Esc closes. Every action in AC11 has a key, and the tab's first line shows those keys. Proven by a keypress-driven test that goes from `/schedules` to a paused schedule without; any mouse event.

AC13: A scheduled run that finishes in another process updates the open TUI without a; restart. The Schedules section, and an open detail modal, poll the ledger and reports on an; injectable interval. They repaint only when the ledger or reports changed. The TUI shows a one-line notice once for each new report. Proven by a test that appends a record and a report to a fixture, fires the injected; timer, and asserts the row and the Runs tab changed and the notice appeared once.

AC14: Every scheduled run is spend-bounded and visible in governance. Before its first model call, a run reserves spend under the project-wide lock, against; the smaller of the project ceiling and the schedule's `ceilingUsd`. Over either ceiling, it records `budget-refused` and calls no model. The sidebar row and; the modal show that outcome. Its closing record in `runs.jsonl` carries the runId, tokens and USD, and it closes the; reservation. `keryx governance report` includes that cost in project trigger spend. Proven by an; extended `governance/report.test.ts` case.

AC15: Documentation is updated, and CI is green with `keryx health run` passing. `docs/docs/cli-reference.md`, `README.md` and the docs site no longer say that keryx only; prints schedules. They document creation with confirmation, grants, installation, list, pause/resume/delete, the sidebar and modal, and reports. They state the honest limits: the machine must be on; a sleeping laptop gets one catch-up run on wake through `Persistent=true`; cron does not catch up; without linger nothing runs while logged out; the hardened sandbox is Linux-only, so macOS schedules are `ask` with granted tools; only. An agent skill tells the agent when to propose `schedule_create`, and that it can never; confirm a schedule itself. CI is green on the branch, and `keryx health run` passes.

flows.title: keryx shell: keep saved provider keys out of MCP server environments
criteria: AC1: When `keryx shell` — or any other surface that starts MCP servers through the shared MCP runtime — launches a server, every environment variable keryx loaded from its saved configuration is removed by name before the server's own configured environment is applied, whatever the variable is called. A test saves a provider key under a custom name that contains none of KEY, TOKEN or SECRET and asserts the launched server does not see it.
AC2: A server whose own configuration names a variable explicitly still receives it: explicit configuration wins over the strip, and a test shows it.
AC3: The ACP path, which already strips saved keys, and the shell path use one shared function rather than two copies, and the existing name-pattern strip keeps working.
AC4: The documentation of MCP servers states which environment a launched server receives and which it does not.
AC5: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: Governance report: unattended-run denials and dispatch runs attributed to their flow
criteria: AC1: `keryx governance report` reads the denials that unattended trigger runs record and lists them per trigger and run — the tool, the reason and the time — instead of reporting every policy decision as not recorded. Policy decisions of interactive sessions, which still have no durable record, are reported as not recorded with that narrower reason.

AC2: A dispatch run that names a flow and task is attributed to that flow in the report — its spend and its outcome — while trigger runs without a flow stay a project-level line; if run records do not yet carry the flow, they gain it additively and older records still read.
AC3: The report no longer describes flow 290 as a future source, and a test pins where the denials come from.
AC4: Tests over a fixture ledger cover a dispatch run with denials, an open spend reservation, a report-only run and a record written before this change.
AC5: The CLI reference describes the new sections of the report.
AC6: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: ACP client stderr budget, docs and agent skills for triggers and external agents
criteria: AC1: The ACP client counts what a foreign agent writes to stderr against a run budget, so a stderr-only flood ends the run with a named reason within that budget rather than running on until the run timeout; a test drives such a flood and asserts the named reason and that the child was killed.

AC2: The agent-facing instructions cover triggers and external agents: how a `flow-next` dispatch is configured, run and inspected and what an unattended run may not do, and how `keryx agents external run` works and what keryx does and does not control. Generated and mirrored copies stay identical, every skill stays under its recorded length ceiling, and `keryx skills verify --bundled` reports no finding.

AC3: The architecture page's diagram of the completion gates either lists the gates `flow complete` evaluates today, including tasks, owner and review, or says plainly that it is a simplification and where the full list lives.
AC4: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` gate is pass.

flows.title: A completion signature an agent cannot make on its own, and a way out of completing
criteria: AC1: `keryx flow confirm <id>` mints a completion confirmation token only when stdin and stdout are both TTYs, the flow is `implemented` (or `in-progress` for a `--merged` completion), and its criteria are frozen and intact; it prints the flow id, title, AC checksum, confirmed-criteria count and PR/head being confirmed, requires a random challenge typed back via `/dev/tty`, and stores only the token's sha256 bound to `{flow id, kind: "complete", acChecksum}` with a TTL — tests cover each refusal (non-TTY, wrong status, unfrozen/tampered AC, wrong challenge) and that the plaintext token never reaches disk.

AC2: A flow opts in via `gates.confirmation: true` — written by `flow init --require-confirmation`, or stamped by `flow init` into new flows when `.metaproject/tasks.config.json` has `completion.require_confirmation: true`; for an opted-in flow, `keryx flow complete` records a `confirmation` gate that fails (and the flow returns to `in-progress`, attempt recorded) unless `--confirm-token` is a valid, unexpired, unused token bound to this flow and its current AC checksum; an expired, reused, other-flow, or pre-AC-change token each fail with a named reason — covered by service tests.

AC3: A token is consumed only on a passing completion, in the same save that appends the `complete` signature; that signature keeps its existing `identity` unchanged and gains an additive `confirmation` field (`mechanism: "terminal-token"`, a hash-prefix `tokenRef` — never the token —, `mintedAt`, `consumedAt`, `boundTo: {kind, acChecksum}`); `flow status`, the `flow complete` "Signed by" note and `keryx governance report` show it, and the `identity.basis` enum is not extended — schema test and docpack schema copy stay byte-consistent.

AC4: No agent path can mint or bypass the token: no MCP or agent-native tool mints one (test enumerates `src/mcp/tools.ts` and the interactive tool roster); a shell command containing `flow confirm` resolves to `ask` under every permission mode including `auto` in keryx's own agent loop, the ACP permission classifier and the supervised-codex elicitation path; `flow confirm` and `flow recover` are refused by the unattended floor (`FORBIDDEN_FLOW_VERBS`), and a command or patch naming the token store is refused as a protected path — each asserted by a unit test.

AC5: `flow complete` never leaves a flow in `completing`: an AC tamper caught during or after the gates (failing and passing paths) and any exception thrown by the merge, pull-request or base-branch gates each record a failed completion attempt naming the cause and return the flow to `in-progress` — tests reproduce all three and assert the on-disk status is `in-progress`, the attempt is recorded, and no `complete` signature exists; AC integrity is still enforced on every later forward transition.

AC6: `keryx flow recover <id> --reason "<why>"` moves a flow from `completing` to `in-progress`, appends a `completion-recovered` history/journal event carrying the reason, the last event before the interruption and whether the AC file is currently intact, and never alters `signatures` or `completionAttempts`; it refuses without `--reason`, from any other status, and while another process holds the flow lock (a running `complete`) — covered by service and CLI tests; `flow status` labels a lock-free `completing` flow as interrupted and names the command.

AC7: Backward compatibility: every existing flow package in this repository loads, validates against the flow-state schema and passes `keryx flow check` unchanged; a flow without `gates.confirmation` reports the confirmation gate `skipped` and completes with exactly the pass/fail outcome it had before; existing signatures (without `confirmation`) render unchanged; no `schemaVersion` bump and no on-read rewrite — asserted by a backward-compat test over a pre-change fixture and a sweep over `.metaproject/flows/*/flow.json`.

AC8: The limits are stated, not implied: a decision record (TM-03, linked from TM-02 §7) and the CLI reference state that the token proves an interactive confirmation step outside the agent's tool roster within the TTL for this AC checksum — not that a human performed it — and name the known bypasses (a pty faked with `script`, forging the hash store, obfuscated command text evading the approval floor, agents running outside keryx supervision, hand-editing the opt-in flag in `flow.json`) and that a human who pastes the token to an agent has delegated the completion; `flow complete`'s note repeats the one-line caveat — checked by a docs test grepping the stated limits. The same decision record states that the existing SAC review-confirmation token (`keryx workspace confirm-review`) has the same limits — its hash store can be forged and its approval floor matched by text — so the docs of that mechanism stop implying more.
AC9: CI is green on the PR and `keryx health run` passes on the branch.

flows.title: TUI: sidebar and modals for the governance report, triggers and external agent runs
criteria: AC1: The TUI sidebar has a Governance section, mounted in `sidebarTop` after the Jobs section by an exported `mountGovernancePanel(otui, renderer, parent, opts) → {refresh, dispose}`. It shows exactly one of five states, read from `readLatestGovernanceReport`: `no report — click to run` when the report is absent. `unreadable — click for reason` when the stored report is malformed or cannot be read; the click opens the modal with the reason and `r` to rebuild, never an automatic rebuild. `running…` while a run is in flight. `last report <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM>`, taken from `generatedAt`. `failed — click to retry` after a failed run. Row text stays within `SIDEBAR_TEXT_WIDTH`. Colours come from theme roles only, so a `/theme` switch recolours them. Proven by a panel test over fixture project directories, one per state.

AC2: Clicking the section, or running `/governance`, while there is no report starts the report in the background. It calls the same `buildGovernanceReport` + `writeGovernanceArtifacts` that bare `keryx governance report` calls, for the current project with no filters. The composer stays usable while it runs. A second click during a run starts nothing. When the run finishes, the section changes to `last report <date>` without a restart, and one toast appears. A thrown error leaves the `failed` state and never a stuck `running…`. The run never starts an agent turn: nothing goes through the JobRegistry or a task-notification. Proven by a test with a deferred report builder and a fixture project. It asserts the state sequence and that `latest.json`/`latest.md` were written with `schemaVersion` and the CLI's markdown rendering.

AC3: Clicking the section in the `last report` state, or running `/governance` when a report exists, opens a report modal through `modal-host`. The header shows `generated_at`, the filters and `all_projects` of the stored report. The body is `latest.md`, wrapped to the panel width and windowed. ↑/↓/j/k scroll by a line and PgUp/PgDn by a page, clamped so the last line of a report longer than the body can be reached. `r` re-runs the report in the background. The open modal refreshes when the run finishes. Esc closes the modal. Proven by a keypress-driven modal test over a report of at least three body-heights.

AC4: The TUI sidebar has a Triggers section, mounted after Governance by an exported `mountTriggersPanel`. It is hidden when `.metaproject/triggers.json` is absent. A config that cannot be read shows one error row. The header shows project trigger spend as recorded USD, plus the count of runs whose cost was not recorded, never folded into $0 (`readProjectTriggerSpend`). The number of open spend reservations is shown in the `attention` role. Each event-fired trigger gets one row: name, enabled or disabled, and either the last outcome with its age or `never fired`. A `flow-next` entry whose dispatch has `network: true` carries a `NET` marker in the `attention` role. Schedule-fired entries get no rows, only one `N scheduled` line. This is the seam that leaves them to flow 295's Schedules section. Clicking a row opens that trigger in the modal. Proven by a panel test over a fixture `triggers.json` and `runs.jsonl`.

AC5: `/triggers`, or a click on a Triggers row, opens a list+detail modal through `modal-host`. The detail tab shows: the fire, the action and whether the hook is installed; for a dispatching `flow-next`: provider/model, permission mode, ceiling, max seconds, max attempts, the unattended roster, and network, with the full `NETWORK_ON_WARNING` text when it is on; the last N ledger records, with outcome, cost (`not recorded (<reason>)` when unrecorded), refusal code and denials; every open reservation, with the exact `keryx trigger resolve <runId> --spent <usd>` command. The wording comes from formatters extracted from `src/commands/trigger.ts` and shared with `keryx trigger status/list`, not copied. A test asserts that the CLI and the modal print the same descriptor for the same entry.

AC6: Run-now has one path and cannot do anything the CLI would not. In the Triggers modal, `r` arms run-now on the selected trigger, `y` confirms, and any other key cancels. A disabled or rejected entry cannot be armed, and the modal says why. A confirmed run executes `keryx trigger run <name>` as a child process of the same keryx build the TUI is running (`resolveKeryxInvocation()`, not `keryx` on PATH), in the project root. It is never an in-process call and never a JobRegistry task. The modal shows `running…`, then the new ledger record and the tail of the child's output. Proven by tests on a fixture project: With the maintenance lock held, run-now records `lock-refused`. An `open-flow` over the spend ceiling records `budget-refused`. A `flow-next` dispatch that cannot run records the same `dispatch-refused` code the CLI records. In each case, the ledger record written from the TUI equals the one written by `keryx trigger run` on the same fixture, apart from `at`.

AC7: Work that finishes updates the TUI without a restart, including work done by other processes. One shared, change-detecting watcher, working name `src/tui/trigger-ledger.ts`, is exported for flow 295 to reuse. It polls `runs.jsonl`, `triggers.json` and governance `latest.json` on an injectable interval, and also runs after every settled agent turn. It repaints the Governance section, the Triggers section and an open modal only when one of those files changed. A run the TUI started ends in exactly one toast. Runs started elsewhere repaint silently. Proven by a test that writes a record and a new `latest.json` from outside, fires the injected timer, and asserts that both sections changed and nothing repainted on an unchanged tick.

AC8: Everything is reachable without a mouse, and the commands are registered everywhere they must be. `/governance` and `/triggers` are registered in `AGENT_SLASH_COMMANDS` as agent-mode only. They are listed in `ACP_TUI_ONLY_COMMANDS`. `classifyBusyDispatch` classifies both as read-only while a turn is busy. The registry, busy-dispatch and ACP command tests are updated. Each modal's footer lists its keys. A keypress-driven test with no mouse event goes from the composer through `/triggers` → ↓ → Enter → `r` → `y` to a recorded run, and through `/governance` → `r` to a new report.

AC9: External agent runs are recognisable in the existing sessions UI. The TUI Session Switcher (`/sessions`, `/resume`) already lists sessions written by `keryx agents external run`. A row whose session provider starts with `acp:` shows `acp:<agent>` in its description, and that text is searchable by the filter. Proven by a `sessionPickerOptions` test over an `acp:claude` summary.; and `keryx shell -c` continues the latest session of the shell's own kind, not a session written by `keryx agents external run` (today `latestSession` has no provider filter, so `-c` right after an external run resumes the ACP session) — a test covers it.

AC10: The new sections leave the shell's layout and themes intact. With a fixture project holding a governance report and three triggers, `shell-pty-launch.smoke.test.ts` still finds `Model`, `Context`, `Tools`, `Status` and `Ready` on an 80x24 pty. No new renderable sets `alignSelf`. A `/theme` switch recolours both sections and both modals. The new tests are headless OpenTUI tests (`otui.testing.createTestRenderer`) or fake-renderable panel tests, and they run under `bun run test:client:terminal`.

AC11: Documentation is updated. `docs/docs/cli-reference.md` (the TUI section), `README.md` and the docs site document the Governance and Triggers sidebar sections and their states. They also document both modals and their keys, and `/governance` and `/triggers`. They state that run-now is `keryx trigger run` in a child process, bound by the same locks, budgets and refusals. They state that external agent runs appear in `/sessions`.
AC12: CI is green on the branch, and `keryx health run` passes.

flows.title: Unattended sandbox: an allowlist network mode through the domain proxy on Linux
criteria: AC1: A scheduled `agent-task` grant accepts `network: "allowlist"` with a required non-empty `domains` list (exact names or `*.domain` wildcards, the grammar `matchesAllowlist` already implements); an empty, malformed, IP-literal or bare-`*` entry is refused on load with the reason, the "delivered by flow 301" refusal is gone, and flow-next dispatch keeps its boolean network unchanged.

AC2: `planUnattendedSandbox` with `allowlist` always runs `--unshare-net`, binds no resolv.conf, binds in only the run's proxy unix socket (created under the run's own 0700 scratch parent), and refuses the run - never falls back to `off` or `full` - when the socket or proxy cannot be created.

AC3: The proxy runs outside the sandbox in the dispatcher and listens on that unix socket; it allows plain HTTP by `Host` and HTTPS `CONNECT` by authority only for listed domains, refuses IP-literal targets, and after resolving an allowed name refuses loopback, private, link-local, CGNAT, unique-local and metadata addresses (169.254.169.254 and its encoded forms), reusing or mirroring the coverage in `src/harness/mutation/guard.ts`.

AC4: The proxy connects to the exact address it checked, so a name that resolves to a public address at check time and to a private or metadata address on a second lookup is refused, proven by a test with an injected resolver.

AC5: Inside the sandbox a keryx-shipped TCP-to-unix forwarder, started in the same bwrap invocation as each `shell_exec` command, listens on 127.0.0.1, and HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, http_proxy, https_proxy and ALL_PROXY point at it; bytes a client sends before the unix side connects are not lost.

AC6: A real bwrap integration test on Linux shows `curl` through the proxy reaching an allowed name served by a local test upstream and failing with a proxy refusal for a name not on the list, and a listener on the host's real 127.0.0.1 stays unreachable from inside the sandbox under `allowlist`.
AC7: Every proxy allow and deny decision (host, port, decision, reason, time) is written into the run's report and its runs.jsonl record next to the existing denials and granted calls.
AC8: The domain list is part of the signed schedule content, so changing it after confirmation refuses the run with `grants-changed`, proven by a test.

AC9: The `/schedule` and `schedule_create` confirmation card shows `network: allowlist - <domain>, <domain>` through `cardSafe` and states that only the agent's shell commands are governed, never showing an allowlist as `off` or `full`.
AC10: The TUI Schedules Grants tab and the schedule row show the allowlist mode and every domain, and the Runs tab shows each run's proxy denials, with TUI tests.
AC11: `allowlist` is refused with a reason naming the platform wherever the hardened unattended sandbox is unavailable (macOS, no bwrap), never silently weakened.

AC12: Flow-next dispatch worktrees move under a per-uid 0700 scratch parent that must be ours and not a symlink, as agent-task runs already do, and `planSandbox` there hides that parent from the sandbox, proven by a test that shows one run cannot see another's worktree.

AC13: `keryx sandbox status` keeps the general harness "Domain allowlist" Linux row as not-implemented with a note that the unattended allowlist is a separate capability, so the two surfaces do not disagree silently.

AC14: `docs/docs/cli-reference.md`, `docs/docs/limitations.md`, the README and the scheduled-tasks skill document the mode, that it is Linux-only, that it governs only the agent's `shell_exec` traffic (not the model call and not granted tools, which run outside the sandbox), and the limits: clients that ignore proxy variables get no network, and a blind CONNECT relay cannot see SNI or the in-tunnel host.
AC15: CI is green on the pull request and `keryx health run` passes before merge.

flows.title: Documentation revision: README order, shell and provider onboarding, setup docs cross-linked
criteria: AC1: README.md has one quick start, near the top, and places install, first run and the first working session before the deep-dive sections ("The agent harness", "Core capabilities"); the duplicate "## Quick start" block further down is gone, and a test pins that heading order.

flows.title: keryx help: grouped command help in the CLI and a tabbed /help modal in the TUI
criteria: AC1: A single `HELP_GROUPS` table (under `src/standard/`, beside the command registry) orders the onboarding groups - Start here; Connect a model provider; Look and feel; Working in keryx shell; Project knowledge; Managed work; Automation; External agents, ACP and MCP; Maintenance and diagnostics - and places every `CLI_ROUTES` verb and every `AGENT_SLASH_COMMANDS` entry in exactly one group; a test fails on any unplaced, double-placed or unknown entry.
